authors: Yarkoni T, Poldrack RA, Nichols TE, et al.
title: Large-scale automated synthesis of human functional neuroimaging data
method: Text mining of published fMRI articles, automated extraction of reported activation coordinates, and coordinate-based meta-analysis per term (Neurosynth).
population: Published fMRI literature (nearly 6,000 articles in the original release, per search-indexed summaries).
comparison: Studies whose text uses a term frequently vs. studies that do not.
keyFindings: Relatively simple automated text-mining and meta-analysis reproduced results of manually curated fMRI meta-analyses.
The framework produces probabilistic mappings between terms and reported activation locations, which can support rough 'reverse inference' at the level of the literature.
limitations: Automatic coordinate extraction is noisy and does not separate activations from deactivations or distinct contrasts within a paper (see Neurosynth FAQ).
Terms are lexical labels from article text, not validated cognitive states.
Maps summarise the literature; they are not predictions of how any particular stimulus or person's brain will respond. This app therefore does not use Neurosynth maps to drive the display.

verification.notes: The PMC page (PMC3146590) and PubMed were blocked by the build environment's network policy; details confirmed from search records only.

authors: Neurosynth project
title: Neurosynth: Frequently asked questions
method: Project documentation.
comparison: Not applicable.
keyFindings: 'Uniformity test' maps show how consistently studies that use a term report activation in each voxel; 'association test' maps show whether activation is more likely in studies that use the term than in studies that do not, which controls for regions (e.g., dorsal medial frontal and lateral prefrontal cortex) that are activated across many tasks.
These maps were previously labelled 'forward' and 'reverse inference' maps, which the FAQ describes as a mistake.

Coordinate extraction and automatic annotation are noisy; the 'lexical assumption' (that term use reflects the cognitive process studied) will fail in many individual cases; extraction can miss or duplicate tables and merge distinct analyses.
limitations: Web documentation, not peer reviewed; content can change over time.

verification.notes: The page itself was blocked by the build environment's network policy; statements summarised from search-engine excerpts of the FAQ page.

authors: Dockès J, Poldrack RA, et al.
title: NeuroQuery, comprehensive meta-analysis of human brain mapping
method: Multivariate text-to-brain model trained on the neuroimaging literature that predicts where in the brain findings are likely to be reported for a text query.
comparison: Not applicable.
keyFindings: Predicts the spatial distribution of reported findings from free text, generalising from well-studied to rarer terms.
limitations: Outputs are predictions of where the literature reports findings, not validated maps for arbitrary queries; eLife peer reviewers cautioned that 'any query' could be misread as license to enter arbitrary terms.
Not used to drive this app's display for that reason.

verification.notes: DOI inferred from the eLife article number (eLife uses 10.7554/eLife.<number>); re-check with the verification script.

authors: Poldrack RA
title: Can cognitive processes be inferred from neuroimaging data?
method: Bayesian analysis of the BrainMap database to quantify reverse inference.
comparison: Language vs. non-language studies reporting activation in Broca's area.
keyFindings: Inferring a cognitive process from activation in a region ('reverse inference') is not deductively valid; its usefulness depends on how selectively the region responds.
Using BrainMap, P(language | activation in Broca's area) was about 0.69 - informative but far from certain.
limitations: Estimates depend on the database composition at the time.

authors: Logothetis NK
title: What we can do and what we cannot do with fMRI
method: Review of the physiological basis of the BOLD signal.
comparison: Not applicable.
keyFindings: fMRI measures haemodynamic changes that follow neural activity, not neuronal firing directly; these signals constrain how fMRI data can be interpreted.
Conclusions drawn from fMRI often ignore the method's limitations.
limitations: Review; does not itself test stimulus-region associations.

authors: Belin P, Zatorre RJ, Lafaille P, Ahad P, Pike B
title: Voice-selective areas in human auditory cortex
method: fMRI during passive listening.
stimuli: Vocal sounds (speech and non-speech) and non-vocal environmental sounds; scrambled voices and amplitude-modulated noise as controls.
comparison: Vocal vs. non-vocal sounds and acoustic controls.
keyFindings: Regions along the upper bank of the superior temporal sulcus, bilaterally, responded more to vocal sounds (speech or non-speech) than to non-vocal environmental sounds and matched controls.
limitations: Laboratory sound clips, not continuous naturalistic media.
Sample size not verified in this environment.

authors: Pernet CR, McAleer P, et al.
title: The human voice areas: Spatial organization and inter-individual variability in temporal and extra-temporal cortices
method: fMRI block design, passive listening; individual and group analyses.
stimuli: 8-s blocks of vocal sounds from 47 speakers (speech in several languages plus laughs, cries, coughs) vs. non-vocal sounds; silence blocks.
comparison: Vocal vs. non-vocal sounds.
keyFindings: 94% of participants showed bilateral patches responding more to vocal than non-vocal sounds along the superior temporal sulcus/gyrus.
Three 'voice patches' along the STG/STS were reproducible within individuals but their exact locations varied between individuals.
The extended voice network included the amygdala and prefrontal cortex.
limitations: Block design with short clips rather than continuous media.
Individual variability means a group-level location does not describe any one person.

authors: Norman-Haignere S, Kanwisher NG, McDermott JH
title: Distinct Cortical Pathways for Music and Speech Revealed by Hypothesis-Free Voxel Decomposition
method: fMRI responses to many natural sounds decomposed into components without prior functional hypotheses.
stimuli: 165 natural sounds (speech, music, and everyday sounds).
comparison: Response profiles across sound categories; acoustic feature controls.
keyFindings: Six components explained voxel responses across auditory cortex; four reflected acoustic features (frequency, spectrotemporal modulation, pitch).
Two components were selective for music and for speech respectively, were not explained by standard acoustic features, and were concentrated in distinct regions of non-primary auditory cortex.
limitations: Small sample (n=10) scanned extensively.
Short 2-s clips rather than long-form media.

authors: Norman-Haignere SV, et al.
title: A neural population selective for song in human auditory cortex
method: Intracranial recordings in patients, component decomposition, with fMRI used to map spatial distribution.
population: Neurosurgical patients (intracranial electrodes) plus fMRI participants.
stimuli: Natural sounds including speech, instrumental music and song.
comparison: Response components across sound categories.
keyFindings: Identified a response component that responded nearly exclusively to music with singing, not explained by standard acoustic features, located near speech- and music-selective responses.
limitations: Patient population with clinically placed electrodes; limited spatial coverage.
Single study.

authors: Uppenkamp S, Röhl M
title: Human auditory neuroimaging of intensity and loudness
method: Review of auditory fMRI studies of sound level and loudness.
stimuli: Mostly tones and noise at controlled sound pressure levels.
comparison: Different sound levels.
keyFindings: Increasing sound intensity generally increases BOLD responses across auditory cortex, including Heschl's gyrus and the planum temporale.
Activity in primary and secondary auditory cortex appears to track perceived loudness rather than physical intensity alone.
limitations: Narrative (not systematic) review.
Studies control the level at the ear; this app only sees relative level in the file and cannot know playback volume.

authors: Hamilton LS, Edwards E, Chang EF
title: A Spatial Map of Onset and Sustained Responses to Speech in the Human Superior Temporal Gyrus
method: High-density intracranial recordings (electrocorticography) with data-driven clustering.
comparison: Onset vs. sustained response profiles.
keyFindings: A caudal (posterior) zone of the superior temporal gyrus responded to acoustic onsets, while a rostral-surround zone showed sustained, delayed responses to ongoing speech.
Onset responses could decode sentence and phrase onset boundaries.
limitations: Clinical population with limited electrode coverage.
Speech stimuli; onset responses to non-speech sounds in media are an extrapolation.

authors: Downar J, Crawley AP, Mikulis DJ, Davis KD
title: A multimodal cortical network for the detection of changes in the sensory environment
method: Event-related fMRI.
stimuli: Changes in visual, auditory and tactile stimulation.
comparison: Responses to sensory changes in each modality.
keyFindings: Changes in any modality engaged a right-lateralised multimodal network including the temporoparietal junction, inferior frontal gyrus, insula, and left cingulate and supplementary motor areas; unimodal association cortices responded to changes in their own modality.
limitations: Simple laboratory stimulus changes.
Sample size not verified in this environment.

authors: Kim H
title: Involvement of the dorsal and ventral attention networks in oddball stimulus processing: A meta-analysis
method: Meta-analysis of neuroimaging oddball studies.
stimuli: Deviant stimuli within streams of repeated standards (auditory and visual; task-relevant and task-irrelevant).
comparison: Oddball vs. standard stimuli.
keyFindings: Ventral attention network regions were strongly and largely supramodally associated with oddball effects.
The bilateral inferior frontal junction (dorsal network) was strongly associated with oddball effects.
Oddball effects also appeared in sensory cortices and subcortical regions including putamen and thalamus.
limitations: Oddball paradigms are repetitive laboratory sequences; abrupt events in media differ in context and predictability.

authors: Koelsch S
title: A coordinate-based meta-analysis of music-evoked emotions
method: Coordinate-based meta-analysis of neuroimaging studies of music-evoked emotion.
stimuli: Music intended or reported to evoke joy, sadness, fear, tension, frissons, surprise, unpleasantness, or beauty.
comparison: Emotion-evoking vs. comparison music or conditions (varied across studies).
keyFindings: Music-evoked emotions with positive valence involved a reward network including the ventral striatum (including nucleus accumbens), dorsal striatum, amygdala, anterior cingulate cortex, orbitofrontal cortex, insula, mediodorsal thalamus and secondary somatosensory cortex.
The anterior hippocampus was also implicated in music-evoked emotions.
limitations: Pooled studies differ in emotions targeted and comparisons.
Findings concern people who experienced (or were expected to experience) emotions; media alone does not establish that a listener does.

authors: Mas-Herrero E, Maini L, Sescousse G, Zatorre RJ
title: Common and distinct neural correlates of music and food-induced pleasure: A coordinate-based meta-analysis of neuroimaging studies
method: Coordinate-based meta-analysis comparing music- and food-induced pleasure.
comparison: Pleasure-related contrasts; music vs. food.
keyFindings: Music and food reward robustly engaged overlapping regions of reward circuitry, with differences in intensity and location and additional reward-type-specific activity in sensory and learning-related regions.
limitations: Concerns pleasure reported by listeners; not inferable from the music itself.

authors: Salimpoor VN, Benovoy M, Larcher K, Dagher A, Zatorre RJ
title: Anatomically distinct dopamine release during anticipation and experience of peak emotion to music
method: [11C]raclopride PET with psychophysiological measures, plus fMRI with the same stimuli and listeners.
stimuli: Music that participants found intensely pleasurable.
comparison: Pleasurable vs. neutral music; anticipation vs. peak periods.
keyFindings: Endogenous dopamine release in the striatum at peak emotional arousal during music listening.
fMRI showed a dissociation: caudate more involved during anticipation, nucleus accumbens during peak emotional responses.
limitations: Small, selected sample of listeners using music they chose; sample size not verified here.
Dopamine was measured with PET in those listeners. Nothing in uploaded media can indicate dopamine release, so this app never displays it.

authors: Pereira CS, Teixeira J, et al.
title: Music and emotions in the brain: familiarity matters
method: Passive listening fMRI with personalised stimuli selected from each participant's familiarity and liking ratings.
comparison: Familiar vs. unfamiliar; liked vs. disliked.
keyFindings: Limbic, paralimbic and reward-circuit regions were more active for familiar than unfamiliar music.
Liked vs. disliked music produced smaller differences (cingulate and frontal regions including motor cortex and Broca's area).
limitations: Single study; sample size not verified here.
Shows that listener familiarity changes responses - a factor this app cannot observe.

authors: Grahn JA, Brett M
title: Rhythm and Beat Perception in Motor Areas of the Brain
method: Behavioural rhythm reproduction plus fMRI.
stimuli: Rhythmic sequences with and without a regular beat.
comparison: Beat-inducing (integer-ratio, regular accents) vs. other rhythms.
keyFindings: Rhythms that induce a regular beat elicited higher activity in the basal ganglia and supplementary motor area, consistently across levels of musical training.
Musicians showed additional premotor activity unrelated to rhythm type.
limitations: Simple laboratory rhythms rather than full music.
Sample size not verified here.

authors: Kasdan AV, Burgess AN, et al.
title: Identifying a brain network for musical rhythm: A functional neuroimaging meta-analysis and systematic review
method: Systematic review and coordinate-based meta-analysis of fMRI studies of musical rhythm.
comparison: Rhythm processing contrasts.
keyFindings: Rhythm processing engaged a bilateral sensorimotor network including inferior frontal gyri, supplementary motor area, superior temporal gyri/temporoparietal junction, insula, intraparietal regions and putamen.
Beat-based rhythms were localised more specifically to the bilateral putamen.
limitations: Mostly controlled rhythm stimuli; findings summarised from search-indexed abstract text.

verification.notes: Specific localisation statements were summarised by the search engine from meta-analysis literature; confirm against the abstract with the verification script.

authors: Alluri V, Toiviainen P, Jääskeläinen IP, Glerean E, Sams M, Brattico E
title: Large-scale brain networks emerge from dynamic processing of musical timbre, key and rhythm
method: Acoustic features computationally extracted from a real piece of music and correlated with continuous fMRI time series.
comparison: Voxel time series vs. feature time courses.
keyFindings: Timbral features were associated with cerebellar and sensory/default-mode cortical areas; pulse and tonality features recruited cortical and subcortical cognitive, motor and emotion-related circuits.
limitations: Single piece of music; small sample (not verified here).
Replication (Burunat et al. 2016) found higher-level features less reliable than timbral ones.

authors: Burunat I, et al.
title: The reliability of continuous brain responses during naturalistic listening to music
method: Replication of the Alluri et al. (2012) feature-correlation approach with a similar design and participants.
comparison: Voxel time series vs. musical feature time courses; comparison with the original study.
keyFindings: Responses to low-level (timbral) features replicated more reliably, mainly in auditory cortices; responses to higher-level tonal and rhythmic features were more spatially variable and less consistent.
limitations: Replication claims summarised from search-indexed text.

authors: Koelsch S, Gunter TC, von Cramon DY, Zysset S, Lohmann G, Friederici AD
title: Bach speaks: a cortical "language-network" serves the processing of music
method: fMRI during chord sequences with infrequent unexpected chords.
comparison: Unexpected vs. expected chords.
keyFindings: Unexpected musical events activated Broca's and Wernicke's areas, the superior temporal sulcus, Heschl's gyrus, planum polare and planum temporale, and anterior superior insula - a network previously considered language-specific.
limitations: Group-level overlap does not show that the same neural populations are shared (see Chen et al. 2023).

authors: Chen X, Affourtit J, Ryskin R, Regev TI, Norman-Haignere S, Jouravlev O, Malik-Moraleda S, Kean H, Varley R, Fedorenko E
title: The human language system, including its inferior frontal component in "Broca's area," does not support music perception
method: Individually localised language regions (fMRI) plus patient evidence.
population: Healthy adults and individuals with aphasia.
stimuli: Music and language stimuli including structure manipulations.
comparison: Responses of language-selective regions to music vs. language.
keyFindings: Language regions, including the inferior frontal component in Broca's area, did not support music perception; the authors conclude the two systems are neurally distinct.
limitations: Conflicts with earlier group-level findings of overlap (e.g., Koelsch et al. 2002); differences in methods (individual localisation vs. group averages) likely matter.

authors: Huth AG, de Heer WA, Griffiths TL, et al.
title: Natural speech reveals the semantic maps that tile human cerebral cortex
method: Voxel-wise encoding models of fMRI recorded during hours of narrative stories.
stimuli: More than two hours of stories from The Moth Radio Hour (a storytelling podcast).
comparison: Voxel responses predicted from word-meaning features.
keyFindings: Semantic selectivity was organised in intricate maps spanning temporal, parietal and frontal cortex, with patterns that appeared consistent across individuals - meaning is represented in distributed systems rather than a single module.
limitations: Very small sample (7) scanned for many hours.
Semantic maps were broadly bilateral, whereas meta-analyses of task studies emphasise a left-lateralised network (Binder et al. 2009).

authors: Binder JR, Desai RH, Graves WW, Conant LL
title: Where is the semantic system? A critical review and meta-analysis of 120 functional neuroimaging studies
method: Activation likelihood estimation across semantic processing studies.
stimuli: Words and sentences in semantic vs. control tasks.
comparison: Semantic vs. less semantic conditions.
keyFindings: Semantic processing reliably engaged a distinct, left-lateralised network of 7 regions: posterior inferior parietal lobe, middle temporal gyrus, fusiform and parahippocampal gyri, dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, inferior frontal gyrus, ventromedial prefrontal cortex, and posterior cingulate gyrus.
limitations: Mostly single words and tasks rather than continuous listening.

authors: Lerner Y, Honey CJ, Silbert LJ, Hasson U
title: Topographic mapping of a hierarchy of temporal receptive windows using a narrated story
method: fMRI inter-subject reliability for an intact story and versions scrambled at word, sentence and paragraph scales.
comparison: Intact vs. scrambled story.
keyFindings: Auditory and language areas showed a hierarchy of 'temporal receptive windows': early auditory regions responded reliably even to scrambled speech, while higher-order regions responded reliably only when information was coherent over longer timescales (sentences, paragraphs).
limitations: Single story; sample size not verified here.

verification.notes: Detailed description of the hierarchy (which regions required longer coherence) is from curator knowledge of the paper consistent with the search-indexed abstract; confirm on full text.

authors: Vagharchakian L, Dehaene-Lambertz G, Pallier C, Dehaene S
title: A temporal bottleneck in the language comprehension network
method: Time-resolved fMRI with sentences compressed to different rates.
stimuli: Spoken and written sentences at 20-100% of natural duration.
comparison: Compression rates from intelligible to unintelligible.
keyFindings: A left-hemisphere, modality-independent language network (including inferior frontal gyrus and superior temporal sulcus) showed a remarkably stable response across intelligible rates, then collapsed for unintelligible (20%) sentences.
limitations: Artificially compressed sentences; applies to speech rate only indirectly.

authors: Lipkin B, Tuckute G, Affourtit J, et al.
title: Probabilistic atlas for the language network based on precision fMRI data from >800 individuals
method: Probabilistic atlas built from individual fMRI language localiser maps.
stimuli: Validated language localiser (sentences vs. control conditions).
comparison: Language vs. control conditions, per individual.
keyFindings: Provides, for each location in common space, the probability that it belongs to the language network, reflecting both consistent fronto-temporal topography and substantial individual variability.
limitations: Localiser task, not naturalistic media.
Atlas data are not bundled here; this app highlights broad gyral regions instead.

verification.notes: The description of fronto-temporal topography is curator knowledge consistent with the search-indexed abstract.

authors: Mar RA
title: The neural bases of social cognition and story comprehension
method: Activation likelihood estimation meta-analyses of theory-of-mind (story-based and non-story) and story comprehension studies.
comparison: Theory-of-mind vs. control conditions; story comprehension vs. control.
keyFindings: A core mentalizing network (medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate/precuneus, bilateral temporoparietal junction, plus additional areas) emerged across story-based and non-story ToM studies and overlapped with story comprehension.
limitations: Number of included studies not verified here.

authors: Schurz M, Radua J, Aichhorn M, Richlan F, Perner J
title: Fractionating theory of mind: a meta-analysis of functional brain imaging studies
method: Meta-analysis across groups of theory-of-mind tasks.
stimuli: Various theory-of-mind tasks (false belief, trait judgement, animations, etc.).
comparison: ToM vs. control conditions, by task group.
keyFindings: All task groups overlapped in medial prefrontal cortex and bilateral posterior temporoparietal junction, with task-specific differences elsewhere.
limitations: Laboratory ToM tasks; mental-state words in a transcript are only a weak cue that such reasoning is invited.

authors: Baldassano C, Chen J, Zadbood A, Pillow JW, Hasson U, Norman KA
title: Discovering Event Structure in Continuous Narrative Perception and Memory
method: Data-driven event segmentation model applied to fMRI during a TV episode and recall.
stimuli: An episode of the TV series Sherlock (continuous viewing) and its free recall.
comparison: Model-derived event boundaries vs. human-annotated boundaries; perception vs. recall.
keyFindings: A nested hierarchy of events: short events in sensory regions, long events in higher-order areas including angular gyrus and posterior medial cortex.
High-order event boundaries were coupled to increases in hippocampal activity, which predicted later reinstatement during recall.
limitations: Single stimulus; sample size not verified here.

authors: Yeshurun Y, Swanson S, Simony E, Chen J, Lazaridi C, Honey CJ, Hasson U
title: Same Story, Different Story: The Neural Representation of Interpretive Frameworks
method: Two groups heard the same story after being given different beliefs about it; inter-subject response similarity compared.
comparison: Same stimulus, different interpretive framing.
keyFindings: Responses in higher-order areas - including the default-mode network, language areas and parts of the mirror neuron system - were similar among people sharing an interpretation and differed from those with the opposing interpretation, even though the sound was identical.
limitations: Single narrative; sample size not verified here.
Directly shows that identical media can produce different brain responses depending on the listener's beliefs.

authors: Hasson U, Nir Y, Levy I, Fuhrmann G, Malach R
title: Intersubject Synchronization of Cortical Activity During Natural Vision
method: Free viewing of a feature film during fMRI; inter-subject correlation and reverse correlation.
stimuli: Thirty minutes of a popular feature film.
comparison: Voxel time courses across individuals; reverse correlation to the film frames.
keyFindings: Voxel-by-voxel activity synchronised across viewers in visual and auditory areas and in association cortex.

Part of the shared activity was a widespread pattern correlated with emotionally arousing scenes; part was regionally selective - e.g., face-selective fusiform cortex responded to faces within the unconstrained movie.
limitations: Very small sample (5).
Face/scene selectivity details are summarised from secondary search excerpts.

authors: Kanwisher N, McDermott J, Chun MM
title: The Fusiform Face Area: A Module in Human Extrastriate Cortex Specialized for Face Perception
method: fMRI localiser and control comparisons.
stimuli: Photographs of faces, objects and control images.
comparison: Faces vs. objects and other controls.
keyFindings: A region of the fusiform gyrus in 12 of 15 participants responded significantly more to faces than to common objects; control conditions argued against attention or general animacy explanations.
limitations: Static photographs; not all participants showed the region.

authors: Zhen Z, et al.
title: Quantifying interindividual variability and asymmetry of face-selective regions: a probabilistic functional atlas
method: Individual face-selective region localisation and probabilistic atlas construction.
comparison: Faces vs. control categories.
keyFindings: Six face-selective regions in occipitotemporal cortex, with considerable interindividual variability and rightward asymmetry in selectivity, volume and location.
limitations: Localiser stimuli, not naturalistic video.
Authors after the first two not verified here.

authors: Epstein R, Kanwisher N
title: A cortical representation of the local visual environment
method: fMRI with scene and object stimuli.
stimuli: Photographs of scenes (including empty rooms), objects and faces.
comparison: Scenes vs. objects and faces.
keyFindings: A region of parahippocampal cortex (the 'parahippocampal place area') responded selectively to passively viewed scenes, weakly to single objects and not to faces; spatial layout was the critical factor (empty rooms responded as strongly as complex scenes).
limitations: Static photographs.
Sample size not verified here.

authors: Epstein RA, Baker CI
title: Scene Perception in the Human Brain
method: Review of neuroimaging and neuropsychological studies of scene perception.
stimuli: Scenes (places, landscapes, rooms) in many studies.
comparison: Scenes vs. other visual categories.
keyFindings: Three cortical regions respond selectively to scenes: the parahippocampal place area, the retrosplenial complex/medial place area, and the occipital place area.
limitations: Narrative review; does not quantify effect sizes across studies.

authors: Bartels A, Zeki S, Logothetis NK
title: Natural Vision Reveals Regional Specialization to Local Motion and to Contrast-Invariant, Global Flow in the Human Brain
method: Visual changes in feature films decomposed into global flow (camera/self motion), local flow (object motion) and residual changes (e.g., illumination) and correlated with fMRI.
comparison: Voxel time courses vs. motion and residual-change regressors.
keyFindings: Motion activated V5+/MT+, V3A, medial posterior parietal cortex and, weakly, lateral occipital cortex.
Early visual areas responded only to residual changes (e.g., illumination), not to equally large motion-induced changes.
limitations: Sample size not verified here.
This app's motion measure is a coarse frame-difference/block-matching proxy that does not cleanly separate camera motion, object motion and lighting change.

authors: Zeki S, Watson JD, Lueck CJ, Friston KJ, Kennard C, Frackowiak RS
title: A direct demonstration of functional specialization in human visual cortex
method: PET measurement of regional cerebral blood flow with statistical parametric mapping.
comparison: Motion vs. stationary and colour vs. grey displays.
keyFindings: Distinct regions of human prestriate visual cortex were specialised for different visual attributes, including a region for visual motion (V5).
limitations: Early PET study with coarse resolution.
Sample size not verified here.

authors: Wandell BA, Dumoulin SO, Brewer AA
title: Visual Field Maps in Human Cortex
method: Review of fMRI visual field mapping.
comparison: Not applicable.
keyFindings: Much of human visual cortex is organised into visual field maps, including medial occipital V1-V3, lateral occipital maps (LO-1, LO-2, hMT+), ventral occipital, dorsal occipital (V3A/B) and posterior parietal maps.
limitations: Review of mapping studies; not a measure of responses to any particular video.

authors: Zacks JM, Braver TS, Sheridan MA, et al.
title: Human brain activity time-locked to perceptual event boundaries
method: fMRI during viewing of everyday activities; participants later segmented the same movies.
comparison: Activity at perceived event boundaries vs. other time points.
keyFindings: A network of brain regions responded at perceptually salient event boundaries, both during intentional segmentation and during naive passive viewing.
limitations: Specific regions not verified in this environment; used here only for the general event-boundary claim.

authors: Magliano JP, Zacks JM
title: The impact of continuity editing in narrative film on event segmentation
method: Viewers segmented a commercial film into events; fMRI recorded during viewing.
comparison: Edits continuous in space/time/action vs. discontinuous in space/time vs. discontinuous in action.
keyFindings: Action discontinuities were the strongest predictors of perceived event boundaries; once situational discontinuities were controlled, cuts per se were not positively associated with boundaries.
Posterior regions that increased in activity at continuity edits (early visual cortex, precuneus and lateral regions) overlapped with regions that increase at event boundaries.
limitations: Single film.
Shows that a detected cut is not the same as a perceived event boundary.

authors: Ben-Yakov A, Henson RN
title: The Hippocampal Film Editor: Sensitivity and Specificity to Event Boundaries in Continuous Experience
method: fMRI during film viewing; boundaries identified by independent observers.
comparison: Hippocampal responses at observer-identified event boundaries vs. other moments.
keyFindings: Hippocampal activity was sensitive to event boundaries identified by observers during continuous viewing.
limitations: An erratum (J Neurosci 2021, PMID 33558435) corrected an error in how boundaries were aggregated across observers.
Sample size not verified here.

authors: Lindquist KA, Wager TD, Kober H, Bliss-Moreau E, Barrett LF
title: The brain basis of emotion: a meta-analytic review
method: Meta-analysis comparing locationist and psychological-constructionist accounts of emotion.
stimuli: Varied emotion inductions and perception tasks.
comparison: Discrete emotion categories.
keyFindings: Evidence did not support discrete emotion categories consistently and specifically corresponding to distinct brain regions; e.g., not all instances of fear were accompanied by increased amygdala activity. Findings fit better with emotions constructed from general-purpose networks.
limitations: Theoretical interpretation remains debated (published with open peer commentary).

authors: Farkas AH, et al.
title: Humor and emotion: Quantitative meta analyses of functional neuroimaging studies
method: Quantitative meta-analyses of fMRI humor studies.
population: Published fMRI humor studies (57 per search-indexed summary).
comparison: Humorous vs. non-humorous conditions; comprehension vs. appreciation stages.
keyFindings: Humor comprehension (incongruity detection/resolution) was associated with inferior frontal gyrus, medial and superior frontal gyrus, middle temporal gyrus and inferior parietal lobule.
Humor appreciation was associated with ventromedial prefrontal cortex, amygdala, anterior insula and midbrain; clear nucleus accumbens activity was not identified despite common assumptions.
limitations: Author list beyond the first author and study count come from secondary summaries; confirm with the verification script.
Whether a listener finds something funny is not observable from media.

authors: Moran JM, Wig GS, Adams RB, Janata P, Kelley WM
title: Neural correlates of humor detection and appreciation
method: Event-related fMRI time-locked to humorous moments in full TV episodes.
stimuli: Full-length episodes of the sitcoms Seinfeld or The Simpsons.
comparison: Humor detection moments and humor appreciation moments vs. other moments.
keyFindings: Humor detection moments: increases in left inferior frontal and posterior temporal cortex.
Humor appreciation moments: increases in bilateral insular cortex and amygdala.
limitations: Single study; sample size not verified here.

authors: Vrticka P, Black JM, Reiss AL
title: The neural basis of humour processing
method: Perspective/review of humour neuroimaging.
comparison: Not applicable.
keyFindings: Humour engages a core network: temporo-occipito-parietal areas for detecting and resolving incongruity, and mesocorticolimbic reward structures plus the amygdala for reward and salience.
limitations: Narrative review; its reward-system emphasis is partly qualified by Farkas et al. 2021.

authors: Naci L, Cusack R, Anello M, Owen AM
title: A common neural code for similar conscious experiences in different individuals
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
method: fMRI during a suspenseful short film; suspense rated every 2 s by a separate group.
population: Healthy adults (three groups) and one behaviourally unresponsive patient.
n: 15 in the suspense-rating group (per search-indexed summary); fMRI group sizes not verified
stimuli: An 8-minute edited Alfred Hitchcock TV episode ('Bang! You're Dead').
comparison: Brain activity vs. moment-to-moment group suspense ratings.
keyFindings: Group-averaged suspense ratings predicted activity in a network of frontal and parietal regions; the authors attribute this to the executive demands of following the plot.
limitations: One film; suspense ratings came from a different group than the scanned viewers.

authors: Bezdek MA, Gerrig RJ, Wenzel WG, Shin J, Pirog Revill K, Schumacher EH
title: Neural evidence that suspense narrows attentional focus
method: fMRI while viewing suspenseful film excerpts with flashing peripheral checkerboards.
comparison: Moments of increasing vs. decreasing suspense.
keyFindings: As suspense increased, activity fell in peripheral visual regions along the calcarine sulcus and rose in central visual regions and in frontal and parietal attention regions.
